analysis.one_liner: Forces internet, phone, and TV providers to advertise true total prices and stop surprise fee hikes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee at the end of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies selling internet, phone, wireless, and TV service to advertise the full price a customer actually pays, including taxes, fees, and equipment rental. It would have stopped providers from raising charges mid-contract unless they could show a real cost increase, given 21 days' notice with a penalty-free exit option, and banned billing for services or rented equipment the customer never signed up for. It also would have voided contract clauses that force customers into arbitration instead of court over billing disputes.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy internet, wireless, voice, or pay-TV service — essentially every household. The bill targets the gap between advertised 'promotional' prices and the inflated bills people actually receive, surprise mid-contract rate increases, rental fees for boxes and routers that never improve, junk fees for services never ordered, and forced arbitration clauses that leave customers no practical way to contest bad billing.

how_it_helps.text: Advertised prices would have to include all related taxes, administrative fees, equipment rental fees, and other charges, so the price in the ad would be the price on the bill (with a narrow exception for government taxes that vary by locality).

Providers could not raise total charges during a contract unless they could show an objectively quantifiable cost increase (like a tax or interest-rate change); any increase would require 21 days' advance notice and let the customer cancel without an early termination fee.
Equipment rental fees could not be raised unless the equipment was actually upgraded to provide substantially more functionality — aimed at rising set-top box and router rental charges.

Electronic bills would have to arrive with an itemized breakdown of service charges versus taxes, fees, and rentals, in the same detail as a paper bill, and providers could not bill for services or rented equipment the consumer did not subscribe to or rent.

Contracts could not force customers into arbitration or other alternative dispute resolution over billing disputes — unauthorized charges, unfulfilled promotional rates, or unnotified increases — and any such clause would be void and unenforceable.

analysis.who_pays: Telecom, cable, and wireless providers, whose fee revenue and pricing flexibility would shrink: hidden administrative and equipment fees could no longer pad advertised prices, mid-contract increases would be capped at provable cost changes, and billing disputes would shift from forced arbitration toward court. Providers would also bear compliance costs for itemized e-billing.

drawbacks.text: Banning increases without an 'objectively quantifiable' cost trigger is rigid: a provider could not raise a price to cover genuine but hard-to-quantify costs (like network upgrades or programming fee hikes passed through from content owners) without letting customers exit penalty-free, which could push providers toward higher headline prices instead.

The all-in advertising requirement has a carve-out for government taxes that are 'not uniform throughout the United States,' so local taxes could still make advertised prices understate the true total in many cities.
The ban on compulsory arbitration covers only billing-related disputes defined in the bill; other disputes between customers and providers would remain governed by whatever the contract says.
Providers would face real compliance costs for itemized, emailed billing and price-change notices, which small providers could feel more than large ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the average household, the benefits are direct and recurring: true advertised prices, protection from surprise rate hikes and junk fees, and a workable way to contest erroneous bills. The main costs fall on providers, and the biggest honest criticism is that the cost-increase test in the rate-hike provision is hard to administer and could have unintended effects on how providers price plans. On balance the bill would have shifted bargaining power toward the customer on a set of charges nearly everyone pays.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on September 28, 2018, in the final months of the 115th Congress.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which has jurisdiction over telecommunications.
No further action was ever taken: the record shows no hearing, no committee markup, no report, and no floor vote.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecom, cable, and wireless providers are better off, since their advertised-price practice, fee structures, equipment rental charges, and forced arbitration clauses all remain unchanged. Customers keep paying the gap between advertised and actual prices.

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor, senior member of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole advocate in the record; it died without committee action.

for.name: 16 of 235 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Greg Walden (R-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat for the remaining three months of the Congress and expired.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Cable, broadband, and wireline phone providers (Comcast, Charter, AT&T, Verizon and similar)
industries.note: These companies' revenue depends partly on the gap between advertised promotional prices and all-in bills, hidden administrative fees, and equipment rental charges — exactly what the bill required to be disclosed and constrained. Forced arbitration clauses also keep billing disputes out of court, which the bill would void for billing matters.
Mobile service and mobile data are covered services, so carriers would face the same full-price advertising, rate-increase notice and exit rules, and arbitration ban.

industries.industry: Equipment rental revenue (set-top boxes, gateways, routers)
industries.note: Providers could no longer raise rental fees unless the equipment was actually upgraded with substantially more functionality, a direct constraint on a steadily rising recurring charge on customer bills.
